g001.b_text: Open with the full name of the best-known person, band, game or brand in the fact pack as the very first words of the script, before any number, question or setup.
g001.label: Famous name as first words
g001.text: Open with the full name of the best-known person, band, game or brand in the fact pack as the very first words of the script, before any number, question or setup.
g001.why: Every top Short starts with a recognisable name (The Beatles, Jenna Ortega, Taylor Swift), while flops open with vague teasers like 'You've seen her on screen' or generic topics like octopus blood. Retired unused on 26 October: it is about the opening line, which the hook test covers.

g002.b_text: Put the single most striking number from the fact pack (a time, size, age, rank or count) in the first sentence, attached to what it measures.
g002.label: Headline number in sentence one
g002.text: Put the single most striking number from the fact pack (a time, size, age, rank or count) in the first sentence, attached to what it measures.
g002.why: Top Shorts open with a concrete figure like twelve hours, 27 GB, age 13 or number one, while weak openers such as the Moon and K/DA teasers bury or lack one. Retired unused on 26 October: it is about the opening line, which the hook test covers.

g003.b_text: Follow the first number in the script with a short everyday comparison that makes its scale vivid, such as a working day or a phone's storage, using only facts from the pack.
g003.label: Compare the number to something familiar
g003.text: Follow the first number in the script with a short everyday comparison that makes its scale vivid, such as a working day or a phone's storage, using only facts from the pack.
g003.why: Winners like 12 hours and 27 GB land because the number feels concrete, while weak Shorts leave figures abstract.

g004.b_text: Keep the first sentence to 12 words or fewer and cut any background clause about when, where or what something is, unless that detail is itself the surprise.
g004.label: First sentence 12 words, no background
g004.text: Keep the first sentence to 12 words or fewer and cut any background clause about when, where or what something is, unless that detail is itself the surprise.
g004.why: The weakest openings spend their first seconds on textbook setup like release dates and 'occurs annually', while the strongest get straight to the surprising fact.
